messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to conduct SEM analysis using following model:

model <- "
wm =~ bdk2_sc3 + dsk2_sc3
language =~ grg1_sc1 + vog1_sc3
rxg2_sc3 ~ wm + language + onk2_sc3
language ~ wm
wm ~~ onk2_sc3
"
fit <- sem(model, data = data, group = "language", fixed.x = FALSE)

Wenn I run the fit, following warning came:

Warning message:
In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

It turns out, that the variance of grg1_sc1 is negative (only in one group though). grg1_sc1 is a WLE score and vog1_sc3 is a sum score. Because of problems on data collection I need to use WLE-Score and not the sum score for that particular indicator. Some people told me, that it should not be a problem.
I tried to fix all indicators to 1 and fix residual variance to 0. But it does not solve my problem. Can anyone gives me an advice what I should do?

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: Splitting Dataset by Sex
messages.subject_clean: Splitting Dataset by Sex
messages.body_plain:
On 02/25/2017 06:26 PM, Shubam Sharma wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I have been able to successfully run analyses on SEM models and I am now
> trying to run these analyses separately based on sex. I have tried a few
> different techniques but have not been successful. Here's what I have tried:
>
> 1) Model_Fit <- sem(Model, data=interaction, missing="ML", group = "Sex")

The canonical way to do this would be to subset your data, as in

Model_Fit <- sem(Model, data=subset(interaction, Sex == "male"),
missing="ML")

If that gives you trouble, something along the lines of:

COV <-  cov( subset(interaction, Sex == "male")[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4")] )

where "x1","x2","x3",... needs to be replaced by the variables you wish
to include your analysis. These should be numeric only!

Then, you can inspect this covariance matrix by using

eigen(COV)$values

If all values are positive, then at least the analysis should work for
this group using listwise deletion.

If you keep having trouble, please post the full R script you are using,
and perhaps a snippet of the data.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Suggestion of further development
messages.body_plain:
Yes, RAMONA is a treasure, and lavaan should adopt some of its features.
Please (re)post this as an issue on lavaan's github page.

Yves.

On 02/17/2017 01:35 AM, Jae wrote:
> Dear Yves,
>
> I greatly appreciate your work! lavaan is definitely a wonderful gift to
> the community of researchers around the world.
>
> May I make a suggestion if this is not in the list of future development?
>
> As we know, the usual purpose of SEM is to make sense of relationships
> among manifest variables (MVs) based on a theory about latent variables
> (LVs). In most situations, scales of variables (not only LVs but even
> MVs) are not of primary interest, and this is why some people who know
> what SEM is about want to just look at standardized parameters and their
> corresponding SEs and CIs. For example, RAMONA in SYSTAT, an SEM
> software package that people no longer use much but is otherwise
> technically meticulous, reports all standardized parameters *along with*
> their correct SEs, CIs, and test statistics.
>
> With lavaan, this is not possible. Note that correct SEs and CIs for
> parameters with all variables standardized are not obtained simply by
> applying some formulas to fitted results. The parameterization should be
> different in order to obtain correct results. The idea (which is
> implemented in RAMONA, for example) is that equality constrains are
> imposed on the variances of all endogenous variables (both LVs and MVs).
> Of course, you cannot directly set them to 1 since they are endogenous.
> Instead, these constraints are imposed on the parameters influencing the
> endogenous variables. In the case of MVs, you need to insert sort of
> pseudo-LVs as indicators of each MV and estimate nuisance factor
> loadings to account for MVs' variances. The residual variances of MVs
> are set to 0, and instead, error terms are attached to these pseudo-LVs.
>
> As far as I know, this is the only way to obtain correct SEs and CIs for
> fully standardized parameters.
>
> -Jae
>
> P.S. Not only that, the current way of standardizing endogenous LVs in
> lavaan make parameters around them difficult to interpret.
>

> --

> Groups "lavaan" group.

messages.body_plain:
> Error in nlminb(start = start.x, objective = minimize.this.function, gradient = GRADIENT,  :
>
>   NA/NaN gradient evaluation
>
> I did not understand the error.

nlminb() is the optimizer that searches for a set of parameter estimates that minimize the fit function.  The error means your model did not converge on a solution.

> > summary(fit.madanL, fit.measures = TRUE)
>
> It gave another error:
>
> Error in summary(fit.madanL, fit.measures = TRUE) :
>
>   'fit.madanL' object can not be found.

Because of the previous error, that object was not created.  R cannot find it because it is not there.

> If so, how can I do PCA with R for a data with mostly categorical items (16 out of 19)?

PCA assumes multivariate normality (at least implicitly, as it is applied), so it would not be appropriate.  Yves advice was not to change your hypothesized model by permanently reducing the number of items.  What you should do is simply choose 3 items and fit a 1-factor CFA (it will be just identified).  From there, start building up the model slowly by adding an item at a time for the same factor, then 3 items for another factor, and add one more at a time... The goal is not to interpret those models, but to try to find out the practical limits of your data by seeing when the convergence problems start happening.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: What does check="start" do?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

unfortunately, I Google and searching the archives of this list didn't answer the following question regarding the check="start" option for cfa() in lavaan.

I have fitted a complex CFA model using lavaan (a multistate-multitrait model of six item-specific traits at two time points), which yields nonpositive definiteness ("WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite"). When I include check="start" in the options, this warning no longer shows, but I'm not quite sure a) what this option does; b) whether this means that the original problem has been resolved (or that merely the warning message has disappeared). If somebody could explain the option or point me to a relevant source, I'd be grateful for that.

Reproducible example:
library(lavaan)
model <- readLines(url("https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/66464491/model.txt"))
data <- read.table(url('https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/66464491/msmt-data.csv'))
fit <- cfa(model, data=data, missing="fiml") # warning: nonpositive definite
fit1 <- cfa(model, data=data, missing="fiml", check="start") # no warning

Kind regards,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

Today I estimated a latent baseline-change, and a latent neighbor change model with the cfa-function in lavaan.

Comparing my results to the corresponding latent state model everything seemed fine (same model fit, latent state intercepts were replicated by the baseline and change intercepts).

In a second step I introduced a manifest predictor (intervention: 0 = control group, 1 = intervention group).

In the baseline change model the correlations between the change-residuals were still estimated but not the correlations between the baseline-residual and the change-residuals.

In the neighbor change model neither the correlations between the change-residuals, nor the correlations between the baseline-residual and the change-residuals were estimated.

Is there a reason for this difference and for the restriction of correlations between the baseline and changes factor residuals?

Thanks a lot!

Elisabeth

ltw2 <- function (object, constraints = NULL, verbose = FALSE)
{
    if (object@optim$npar > 0L && !object@optim$converged)
        stop("lavaan ERROR: model did not converge")
    if (is.null(constraints) || nchar(constraints) == 0L) {
        stop("lavaan ERROR: constraints are empty")
    }
    PT <- as.data.frame(object@ParTable, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    eq.idx <- which(PT$op == "==")
    if (length(eq.idx) > 0L) {
        PT <- PT[-eq.idx, ]
    }
    partable <- as.list(PT)
    FLAT <- lavParseModelString(constraints)
    CON <- attr(FLAT, "constraints")
    LIST <- list()
    if (length(CON) > 0L) {
        lhs = unlist(lapply(CON, "[[", "lhs"))
        op = unlist(lapply(CON, "[[", "op"))
        rhs = unlist(lapply(CON, "[[", "rhs"))
        LIST$lhs <- c(LIST$lhs, lhs)
        LIST$op <- c(LIST$op, op)
        LIST$rhs <- c(LIST$rhs, rhs)
    }
    else {
        stop("lavaan ERROR: no equality constraints found in constraints argument")
    }
    theta <- object@optim$x
    ceq.function <- lav_partable_constraints_ceq(partable = partable,
        con = LIST, debug = FALSE)
    JAC <- try(lav_func_jacobian_complex(func = ceq.function,
        x = theta), silent = TRUE)
    if (inherits(JAC, "try-error")) {
        JAC <- lav_func_jacobian_simple(func = ceq.function,
            x = theta)
    }
    if (verbose) {
        cat("Restriction matrix (jacobian):\n")
        print(JAC)
        cat("\n")
    }
    theta.r <- ceq.function(theta)
    if (verbose) {
        cat("Restricted theta values:\n")
        print(theta.r)
        cat("\n")
    }
    VCOV <- vcov(object, labels = FALSE)
    info.r <- JAC %*% VCOV %*% t(JAC)
    Wald <- as.numeric(t(theta.r) %*% solve(info.r) %*% theta.r)
    Wald.df <- nrow(JAC)
    Wald.pvalue <- 1 - pchisq(Wald, df = Wald.df)
    list(stat = Wald, df = Wald.df, p.value = Wald.pvalue, se = object@Options$se)
}

messages.body_plain:
> fit <- cfa(model, data=data, missing="fiml") # warning: nonpositive definite

The default value for 'check' is:

 > lavOptions()$check
[1] "start" "post"

So -by default- both the starting values are checked, and the
post-estimated statistics (ie model implied ov/lv covariances). It is
the latter one that triggers the warning about the nonpositive lv
covariance matrix.

If you specify check="start", you only request "check the starting
values", but not the model-implied ov/lv covariances. Therefore, no warning.

This will trigger the warning again:

fit1 <- cfa(model, data=data, missing="fiml", check="post")

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Interpetation of combined effects
messages.subject_clean: Interpetation of combined effects
messages.body_plain:
Andreia--
     The interaction is not a combined effect, but rather the change in effect of each predictor as the other predictor's value varies. It is common in interaction models to see these sign differences moving from main effect to interaction. To interpret, take the "simple slope" (first derivative of the regression equation) with respect to each predictor.

Simple slope (predation) = -1.13 +.42 * insecticide
Simple slope (insecticide) = -0.48 + .42 * predation

Interpreting these is easier since predation and insecticide are both 0-1. The predation simple slope means that there are two slopes for the predation effect: -1.13 when insecticide is not detected and -1.13+.42 = -.71 when insecticide is present. So predation has a stronger negative effect in those cases where insecticide is not detected.

The insecticide simple slope formula says that the slope for insecticide is -0.48 when predation is 0 and (-.48 + .42) = -.06 (or nearly 0) when predation is 1. So insecticide has almost no effect when predation is present, and predation has a lessened but still relatively large negative effect even when insecticide is present.

My go-to for interpreting interaction effects is a standard regression text like Cohen, Cohen, West and Aiken's (2003) text. It is awesomely readable.

messages.body_plain:
> I'm not sure why the negative Eigenvalues are there if the correlations/covariance aren't indicative of something being wrong... Why is that? And what are potential ways forward?

NPD means there is linear dependency in the matrix, so one row is a linear combination of the other rows.  The ways to check whether a matrix is NPD are negative eigenvalues or a negative determinant.  If you have a symmetric matrix with a negative (or zero, i.e., non-positive) value on the diagonal or a standardized off-diagnonal (i, j) element that exceeds +/-1, then you must have linear dependency.  A Heywood case is a sufficient condition for identifying NPD, not a necessary one (true multicollinearity indicates NPD, such as using a scale total as well as all individual scale items, any one of which is redundant with the remaining variables).

Sometimes, as you add constraints, the sampling variability gets less severe and the estimates based on common parameters might not lead to NPD.  Since this is not lavaan specific, you could find more advice on SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics

# I was trying to understand how lavaan identifies certain models that other programs considered nonidentified

# (I assume lavaan uses certain automated constraints in some cases, which I aimed to find out)

# Next, I became puzzled by differences in SEs that followed from certain model constraints

# I hope someone can help me out here

# Here is what I did

rm(list = ls())

require(lavaan)

# Suppose 4 variables depend on a single factor while a fifth variable predicts this factor

# Also suppose that we were able to observe the 5x5x correlation matrix without any sampling error

# say in a sample of size 500

n<-500

# In addition, suppose variable x5 relates to the common factor only,

# so not to specific factors that influence indicators x1 to x4

# This may yield a correlation matrix like the following

cmata<-matrix(scan(),5,5,TRUE, dimnames<-list(paste("x",1:5,sep=""), paste("x",1:5,sep="")))

  1 .49 .28 .56 .14

  .49 1 .28 .56 .14

  .28 .28 1 .32 .08

  .56 .56 .32 1 .16

  .14 .14 .08 .16 1

# I understand that the SEs are a function of the number of parameters included, so

# the following factor model (scaling in x1 to identify the model), should show larger SEs

model1 <- '

            f1=~l1*x1+x2+x3+x4

            l1==.7

           '

# than in a model in which we fix a second loading

model2 <- '

            f1=~l1*x1+l2*x2+x3+x4

            l1==.7; l2==.7

            '

# which should be larger than the SEs in a model in we fix yet another loading

model3 <- '

           f1=~l1*x1+l2*x2+l3*x3+x4

           l1==.7;l2==.7;l3==.4

           '

# which should be larger than in the model in which all loadings are fixed

model4 <- '

           f1=~l1*x1+l2*x2+l3*x3+l4*x4

           l1==.7;l2==.7;l3==.4;l4==.8

           '

# If we include the predictor, we expect the same pattern, i.e.

# the following model (scaling in x1 to identify the model), should show larger SEs

model5 <- c(model1,'f1~x5')

# than a model in which we fix a second loading

model6 <- c(model2,'f1~x5')

# which should be larger than the SEs in a model in we fix yet another loading

model7 <- c(model3,'f1~x5')

# which should be larger than in the model in which all loadings are fixed

model8 <- c(model4,'f1~x5')

# Check

summary( fit1a <- lavaan(model1,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit2a <- lavaan(model2,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit3a <- lavaan(model3,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit4a <- lavaan(model4,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit5a <- lavaan(model5,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit6a <- lavaan(model6,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit7a <- lavaan(model7,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit8a <- lavaan(model8,sample.cov=cmata,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

# Next suppose that x5 does not only relate to the common factor,

# but also to (a number of the) specific factors that influence indicators x1 to x4

# This may yield a correlation matrix like the following

cmatb<-matrix(scan(),5,5,TRUE,dimnames<-list(paste("x",1:5,sep=""),paste("x",1:5,sep="")))

  1 .49 .28 .56 .21

  .49 1 .28 .56 .14

  .28 .28 1 .32 .03

  .56 .56 .32 1 .16

  .21 .14 .03 .16 1

# The analysis of these data with the model above (the predictor x5 included)

# yields different (biased) estimates of the relation between f1 and x5, of course

# SEs are comparable to the previous results

summary( fit5b <- lavaan(model5,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit6b <- lavaan(model6,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit7b <- lavaan(model7,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit8b <- lavaan(model8,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

# If the relations between specific factors between x1 to xn are randomly distributed around 0

# then including these relationships in the model will remove (or reduce) the bias (was my thinking)

# There's a difficulty however:

# If a remembered correctly the following model would be nonidentified

model5c <- c(model1,'f1~x5;x1+x2+x3+x4~x5')

# But I wanted to know whether fixing additional loadings, would resolve the nonidentification

model6c <- c(model2,'f1~x5;x1+x2+x3+x4~x5')

model7c <- c(model3,'f1~x5;x1+x2+x3+x4~x5')

model8c <- c(model4,'f1~x5;x1+x2+x3+x4~x5')

# Check

# Unexpectedly the first model was already identified; the other were too

# at least... in lavaan (not in Mplus and LISREL, for instance)

# And SEs of the regression coefficients did not depend on the number of parameters included

summary( fit5c <- lavaan(model5c,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit6c <- lavaan(model6c,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit7c <- lavaan(model7c,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

summary( fit8c <- lavaan(model8c,sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

# In Mplus, one needs to fix at least one relation between xi and x5 (e.g., to 0)

I think (!) we can only expect estimating fewer parameters to yield smaller SEs on the condition that the model is correctly specified. If there are omitted nonzero parameters, then the likelihood will not have a nice smooth mound shape, but will be broad and lumpy, due to many possible "best approximations" to the data by a model that is insufficient to account for them.

Perhaps a quick simulation, to see which SEs most closely match the observed variability of estimates?

> # given the model is not identified in Mplus and other software packes,
>
> # How did lavaan eventually identify the model?

Identifiability is a property of the model, not the software, so I expect if the models are truly specified identically, the difference is in the behavior of their optimizers (e.g., nlminb() in R vs. Mplus's optimizer), such as differences in the algorithms or the convergence criteria.  If a model is truly not empirically identified, it is often still possible to find a local solution.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence, thanks for your swift response!

"I think (!) we can only expect estimating fewer parameters to yield smaller SEs on the condition that the model is correctly specified."

I think(!) so too. As you can see I made sure I chose my correlations among x1-x4 such that the one factor model would show perfect fit. (The matrix follows from a standardized single factor model with loadings .7, .7, .4, .8, so that the expected correlation matrix =
loadings%*%diag(4)%*%loadings). There is no sampling error. Next, I chose the constraints such that they equaled the actual values,which ensured fit would still be perfect). The only misfit can come from the relation between on the one hand x5 and on the other hand x1-x4. To study this local misfit was actually first research interest, after which I encountered the automatic identification puzzle/SE problem in lavaan.

"From your description, it looks like you are fixing the wrong parameter: x1~x5 instead of f1~x5.  But I agree, if you fixed the value at its ML estimate, I would expect other point estimates to remain the same and with smaller SEs"

No it is the right one. It was x1~x5 that I initially constrained to 0 and next to the value that lavaan gave earlier, when the parameter was estimated freely.

"Perhaps a quick simulation, to see which SEs most closely match the observed variability of estimates?"

This is exactly the origin of why me and my colleagues wanted to know how lavaan and Mplus differ. We started by such simulations experiments, to investigate how the relation f1~x5 will be biased if some of the x1 and x4 variables also have direct relationships with x5 (next to the indirect relations via f1). Apart from bias, we were also interested in the power to detect the f1~x5 relationship and the number of false positives. Evidently, fixing one of the x1 to x4 direct relationships with x5 will influence the bias, yet the fixation is required to identify the model.

"Identifiability is a property of the model" True, but..

"not the software,"

is not an entirely valid agument, because the software may have built-in additional automated procedures to help identify a model. For example, to help identify the model, lavaan automatically fixes the first factor loading of each factor to 1, unless the user overrides this default n order to identify the model differently. SIMPLIS has built in a similar autmated procedure, but rather than scaling in lamba, SIMPLIS default is to scale in Psi (i.e. SIMPLIS fixes the variance of the factors to 1),  at least when we have a first order factor model. In addition, in lavaan, if a factor only has one indicator specified, this gets detected and the residual variance of the indicator is fixed automatically (to 0). So we know software can have 'hidden' ways to help identify a model. lavaan clearly has it. Mplus, lavaan, (OpenMx) do not have these, as far as I know. In my model, I wanted to know what assumption lavaan makes to identify the model, which - I assume - the program did.

"so I expect if the models are truly specified identically, the difference is in the behavior of their optimizers (e.g., nlminb() in R vs. Mplus's optimizer), such as differences in the algorithms or the convergence criteria."

Also possible, but personally I believe the differences are firstly due to the automated/hidden ways of constraining parameters. I was able to obtain the same parameter point estimates in Mplus once I put explicit constraints to the model. The SEs differed however, so indeed can be optimizer differences. Or... it is the case that the constraints in lavaan yield more precise SEs as compared to the way I constrained the parameters in Mplus. This is a plausible explanation because we got to know that also WITHIN lavaan, the SEs clearly depend on the manner of constraining!

"If a model is truly not empirically identified, it is often still possible to find a local solution."

But here you refer to the problem wether or not the model is empiricallly identified or unidentified. A good general example is when a piece of variance needs to be decomposed in two parts and it happens that piece is 0, so that we can not decompose that piece of variance after all, although in principle we would be able to do so if that variance would have been larger. Specifically, this also happens when there is multicollinearity. Such problems does not appear in the model (I believe). Besides, usually a program will give a warning if this is going on; for example, the program finds a solution, but also mentions that the SEs cannot be computed or should not be trusted. Or the SEs are huge, for instance.
I won't exclude the possibility that the model was empirically unidentified, but I ought the possibility small (especially since lavaan gave smaller SEs in the situation the chances were the greatest this problem might have occurred).

So, all in all I'm still puzzled and still want to know what assumptions lavaan made to identify a model, which I know would not have been identified if not additional assumptions would have been made.

Nevertheless, thanks very much for sharing your thoughts on the topic! It convinced me, I should keep being puzzled :)

Best,
Kees-Jan

messages.subject_clean: CFA Model and Indirect effects
messages.body_plain:
> 1) I recoded gender with dummy coding and the IV with ordinal coding

Your syntax and path diagram have no labels, so I can't tell how these variables operate in your model.  But if they are both exogenous predictors, then dummy codes are necessary for any kind of categorical variable (binary, ordinal, nominal).

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Also, you say you have a moderator, but there are no product terms in your path diagram or syntax.  So neither predictor is a moderator, just a covariate.

> but the DV and the MED2 are frequency raw data, is this problem to fit the model?

If they are not approximately continuous, then they should be treated as counts. Mplus is the only SEM software I am aware of that allows count outcomes.  If there are not very many categories, you could treat the count outcome as ordered.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

> Also the IV is pretty skewed, should I use the MLM estimator?

If you set fixed.x = TRUE (the default option: ?lavOptions), no assumptions are made about the distribution of exogenous predictors.

> 2) I want to control for the clustering effect of the model by city where participants are living in (80 different cities) but R is warning me :
>
> "Warning messages:
> 1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, group.label = group.label,
>   lavaan WARNING: `group.label' argument will be ignored if `group' argument is missing

You did not tell lavaan which column in DF is the grouping variable. You do not need to specify "group.label" unless you want to specify that the cities appear in a particular order in the output.

cfa(model, data=DF, missing='fiml', group = "CITY")

> 2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = model, data = DF, missing = "fiml", group.label = DF$CITY,  :
>   lavaan WARNING: syntax contains parameters involving exogenous covariates; switching to fixed.x = FALSE"
>
> Group involves exogenous covariates? Sorry I do not get that point.

The message is not about group, it is about exogenous covariates (IV and MOD1).  You do not need to specify that they (co)vary in the syntax.  Using fixed.x = TRUE tells lavaan to just use their observed sample statistics, so that you don't need to assume they are normally distributed.

> 3) Finally, once the model has been fitted, Rosseel (2012) precised that we can evaluate indirect effect in mediation analysis. But the fact that we're using CFA/SEM model isn't actually alternative to mediations analysis? Or are they complementary?

You can conduct mediation analysis in many ways.  SEM is one of the better frameworks because all paths are easily estimated simultaenously.  If you have categorical outcomes, though, it gets tricky.  See some later slides in this presentation:

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

You can also find a lot of advice about mediation on SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

FYI, there is no measurement model in your syntax or diagram, so this is a path analysis, not a CFA.  But either the cfa() or sem() functions both call lavaan() with the same default settings, so that detail is inconsequential.  I was just confused by "CFA" in the subject.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

You didn't specify any intercepts in your syntax, and the growth() function only knows how to treat indicators of latent growth factors by default (setting indicator intercepts to zero, and freely estimating intercepts of latent factors). messages.body_plain:
> "From your description, it looks like you are fixing the wrong parameter: x1~x5 instead of f1~x5.  But I agree, if you fixed the value at its ML estimate, I would expect other point estimates to remain the same and with smaller SEs"
> No it is the right one. It was x1~x5 that I initially constrained to 0 and next to the value that lavaan gave earlier, when the parameter was estimated freely.

OK, so you meant x1 instead of f1.  I ran your syntax and saw where the fixed value came from, and I also noticed the SEs increase between models fit8c and fit10c that you saw (sometimes twice as high).

> WITHIN lavaan, the SEs clearly depend on the manner of constraining!

I also found it strange that SEs only changed for regression slopes.  The SEs for loadings and variances were identical (to the third decimal, at least).

> > "not the software,"
>
> is not an entirely valid agument, because the software may have built-in additional automated procedures to help identify a model.

> ...

> > "so I expect if the models are truly specified identically, the difference is in the behavior of their optimizers (e.g., nlminb() in R vs. Mplus's optimizer), such as differences in the algorithms or the convergence criteria."
>
> Also possible, but personally I believe the differences are firstly due to the automated/hidden ways of constraining parameters.

Right, those are differences in default model specification choices, not estimation algorithms.  So I would still describe this as a specification issue, because you are curious about the differences in default specification choices made by different software packages, which is independent of their optimization routines.

> I wanted to know what assumption lavaan makes to identify the model, which - I assume - the program did

You can always consult the parameter table to see exactly what parameters were fixed/free in your fitted model.

parTable(fit5c)

Mplus is not quite as transparent, but you can still tell which parameters were freed by inspecting the nonzero parameter numbers in the TECH1 output.  lavaan provides similar output for easy comparison:

lavInspect(fit5c, "free")

Because lavaan only uses the LISREL matrices, it does not have a separate matrix for effects of exogenous predictors. So to handle x5 predicting f1 (as well as x1-x4), you can see that lavaan automatically "promotes" x1-x5 to latent variables with single indicators, and estimates loadings in Beta like for second-order factors:

lavInspect(fit5c, "est") # lambda is identity for x1-x5, theta is zero

So although the model specification may not be identical, you can still check whether the specifications in lavaan and Mplus are equivalent (such that the two representations would lead to identical model-implied Sigma).  If their specifications are equivalent, I would still assume any difference between their point/SE estimates must be due to differences in the estimation algorithm.

> > "If a model is truly not empirically identified, it is often still possible to find a local solution."
>

> But here you refer to the problem whether or not the model is empiricallly identified or unidentified. ... Such problems do not appear in the model (I believe). Besides, usually a program will give a warning if this is going on; for example, the program finds a solution, but also mentions that the SEs cannot be computed or should not be trusted. Or the SEs are huge, for instance.

Right, like this clearly underidentified model, which even has negative df

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 '
fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, auto.var = TRUE)
lavInspect(fit, "converged") ## no SEs, but still "converged"

But I am not so certain that there isn't some mysterious empirical identification issue.  For instance, if you fit model5c again (that we both assume is underidentified because x5 freely predicts x1-x4 as well as f1), using the model-implied moments from fit5c, you will get the same estimates and SEs.  This is no surprise, given that fit5c perfectly reproduces the data ($\chi^2$ == 0).

summary(fit5c)
summary(update(fit5c, sample.cov = lavInspect(fit5c, "cov.ov"), sample.cov.rescale = FALSE))

But if you identify the measurement model by fixing the factor's (residual) variance instead of the first loading, then you get the expected warning message you mentioned, that SEs could not be computed:

summary(update(fit5c, model = 'f1~x5;  f1=~x1+x2+x3+x4 ; x1+x2+x3+x4~x5', sample.cov = lavInspect(fit5c, "cov.ov"), sample.cov.rescale = FALSE, std.lv = TRUE))

Yet this is a statistically equivalent model, verified by the fact that its chi-squared is also 0, with 1 df.

> I won't exclude the possibility that the model was empirically unidentified, but I ought the possibility small (especially since lavaan gave smaller SEs in the situation the chances were the greatest this problem might have occurred).

Well, we both expected model5c to be underidentified (despite positive df), but it seems to be empirically identified for some reason.  I wondered whether lack of sampling error had anything to do with the optimizer's ability to find a solution, but even if sampling from cmatb, nlminb() finds a solution and computes SEs.

temp <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(500, mu = rep(0, 5), Sigma = cmatb))
summary(update(fit5c, data = temp, sample.cov = NULL))

So I am as stumped as you are.  If you can fit model5c in Mplus and print TECH1 output, perhaps post that output here as an attachment to help verify whether the model specifications are at least equivalent.  I think Mplus will still print TECH1 even if the model does not converge.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Measurement Invariance - comparison of means across groups
messages.subject_clean: Measurement Invariance - comparison of means across groups
messages.body_plain:
> Regarding the two subgroups they are partial strict invariant.

Hopefully that means you have 2 invariant indicators, because there is no way to test whether 1 indicator is invariant (all models with 1 invariant item would be statistically equivalent).  Of course, strict invariance is not required for testing latent parameters anyway.  Only invariant loadings are required for testing latent (co)variances, but intercepts are also required for testing latent means.

> Now I want to compare the latent means of both groups and analyze if they are statistical significant different.
> Furthermore, I want to analyze the correlation between the latent constructs of both groups.
> For this analyze I want to use the SEM. May anyone help me?

Same way, by testing model constraints.  Those parameters should be freely estimated in your partial-strict-invariance model.  So if you fit a model where you add the constraint that latent means are equal (e.g., fixing the means to zero in both groups instead of only the first group), then you test that null hypothesis with a chi-squared difference test returned by anova() or lavTestLRT().  You can constrain a latent mean or covariance to equality across groups by assigning a parameter the same label within each group.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html  (see Constraining a single parameter to be equal across groups)

Or if you only have 2 groups and the latent mean is only estimated in the second, then that parameter estimate is already "how different from zero" it is, so you can look at the Wald z for that parameter to test whether it equals zero (the first group's mean).

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> my first regression line should include:
>
> DV~MOD1*MED1+MOD1*MED2+IV

Term-expansion with the asterisk operator (*) works like that in formula objects (?formula), but lavaan does not use formula objects.  This is because SEMs model several regression equations simultaneously.  So you need to explicitly include the product term as an additional variable in your ?model.syntax, like so:

myData$med1xG <-  myData$MED1 * myData$MOD1
myData$med2xG <-  myData$MED2 * myData$MOD1

model <- '
  # regressions
  DV ~ MOD1 + MED1 + MED2 + med1xG + med2xG + IV
...
'

> Do you recall a way to display R2-squared values for this? (to evaluate how much variance the full model explained).

R-squared for each endogenous variable is the variance explained by its predictors, and you can request that from the summary() or parameterEstimates() output using the argument "rsquare = TRUE".

> What do you mean by "approximately continuous"? Is there a statistical way to check for that?

Not in a hypothesis-testing way, but there are practical guidelines you might be able to find with a little Googling.  I think a Poisson distribution is approximately normalish when the mean is as little as 10 or 15.  Binomial (not binary) variables are approximately normal when they are based on at least 30 trials.  But continuity should be good enough, even if not normal, because there are robust estimators that adjust for excess kurtosis.  Ordinal data can be treated as continuous when there are at least 5 categories, or at least 7 if the distributions are quite skewed.  Here is some helpful reading, although it is about ordinal data, not counts per se.

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

> Yes now the error message referred to something more specific :
>

>   lavaan ERROR: data contains only a single observation in group 9
> In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50) "
>
> I guess lavaan assumed there is at least 2 observations per group?

At least two observations are necessary to calculate (co)variance, because there is no (co)variability in a single number.  But you need a lot more than 2 observations per group in SEM.  How many cities do you have?  If it is more than a 10, a multilevel SEM is probably the framework you want.  lavaan does not yet provide multilevel functionality, but it will eventually (probably slowly) introduce such features:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/development.html

Here are a couple of articles that provide a good conceptual introduction to MSEM:

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3102/1076998616646200

https://www.statmodel.com/download/mehtaneale.PDF

messages.body_plain:
>   lavaan ERROR: sample covariance matrix is not positive-definite

Because you are providing raw data, this probably means that there is linear dependency among your variables (at least, when calculated using complete observations).  You can check the covariance matrix of variables in your data set like this:

myNames <- lavNames(sem(mod_s))
myData <- data_cl[myNames]
myData <- myData[complete.cases(myData), ] # unnecessary if no missing data
myCov <- cov(myData)
round(myCov, 2)
## check whether any correlations are perfect (i.e., collinearity)
myCor <- cov2cor(myCov)
noDiag <- myCor
diag(noDiag) <- 0
any(noDiag == 1)
## if not, check for multicollinearity (i.e., is one variable a linear combination of 2+ variables?)
det(myCov) < 0
## or
any(eigen(myCov)$values < 0)

If you have linear dependency among your variables, then there is redundant information (because one variable is already a combination of other variables, without error).  So you would need to use a subset of nonredundant variables in your analysis.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: increase in SEs while fixing a parameter/model identification in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

Awesome response. Learned a lot from it. Thank you!

I forgot to tell you the results of our simulations (with the presence of sampling error, so no perfect fits). These results were as follows:
- With all factor loadings constrained and all regressions estimated freely (so the model we believe is un- or underidentified and which gives the small SEs), the number of false positives considering the relation between x5 and f1 was ok. The power to detect this relation was also ok (not perfect though). Yet, the estimate b was always biased (underestimated, I believe, I need to ask Dylan Molenaar), so we thought this could be a scaling issue, somehow, perhaps due to the fixing of the factor loadings.
- The same model with additionally one of the regression coefficients fixed (so a model we would normally fit and of which we certainly know it is identified) gave more accurate estimates (at least as we fix the smallest coefficient, of course). But.... the power dropped to detect b dropped dramatically.
- These results of course reflect the small versus ses. But based on our simulations our preliminary conclusion would be that we should trust the SEs of the one model but the point estimate from the other(!). All in all, things boils down to the question why the method of fixing an additional parameters yields larger rather than smaller SEs. I simply don't understand why those SEs in the second model  (1 regression fixed) are so large. On the other hand I have a kind of feeling that this has to do with the (in principle arbitray) choice which of the regression coefficients to fix at 0. I mean, obviously, fixing a large coefficient to 0 would result in large biases of the estimates of the other coefficients.

"But if you identify the measurement model by fixing the factor's (residual) variance instead of the first loading, then you get the expected warning message you mentioned, that SEs could not be computed:"

Well, if you specify your model the way you do. If you specifiy it like this:

model5d <- '
                 f1=~l1*x1+l2*x2+l3*x3+l4*x4
                 f1~~vf1*f1
                 '
summary (lavaan(c(model5d,'vf1==1'),sample.cov=cmatb,sample.nobs=n,auto.fix.first=FALSE,auto.var=TRUE) )

lavaan still gives SEs. This strengthens by belief that lavaan makes some additional assumptions under the hood.

KJ

On Wednesday, March 8, 2017 at 12:32:33 PM UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > "From your description, it looks like you are fixing the wrong parameter: x1~x5 instead of f1~x5.  But I agree, if you fixed the value at its ML estimate, I would expect other point estimates to remain the same and with smaller SEs"
> > No it is the right one. It was x1~x5 that I initially constrained to 0 and next to the value that lavaan gave earlier, when the parameter was estimated freely.
>
> OK, so you meant x1 instead of f1.  I ran your syntax and saw where the fixed value came from, and I also noticed the SEs increase between models fit8c and fit10c that you saw (sometimes twice as high).
>
> > WITHIN lavaan, the SEs clearly depend on the manner of constraining!
>
> I also found it strange that SEs only changed for regression slopes.  The SEs for loadings and variances were identical (to the third decimal, at least).
>
> > > "not the software,"
> >
> > is not an entirely valid agument, because the software may have built-in additional automated procedures to help identify a model.
> > ...
> > > "so I expect if the models are truly specified identically, the difference is in the behavior of their optimizers (e.g., nlminb() in R vs. Mplus's optimizer), such as differences in the algorithms or the convergence criteria."
> >
> > Also possible, but personally I believe the differences are firstly due to the automated/hidden ways of constraining parameters.
>
> Right, those are differences in default model specification choices, not estimation algorithms.  So I would still describe this as a specification issue, because you are curious about the differences in default specification choices made by different software packages, which is independent of their optimization routines.
>
> > I wanted to know what assumption lavaan makes to identify the model, which - I assume - the program did
>
> You can always consult the parameter table to see exactly what parameters were fixed/free in your fitted model.
>
> parTable(fit5c)
>
> Mplus is not quite as transparent, but you can still tell which parameters were freed by inspecting the nonzero parameter numbers in the TECH1 output.  lavaan provides similar output for easy comparison:
>
> lavInspect(fit5c, "free")
>
> Because lavaan only uses the LISREL matrices, it does not have a separate matrix for effects of exogenous predictors. So to handle x5 predicting f1 (as well as x1-x4), you can see that lavaan automatically "promotes" x1-x5 to latent variables with single indicators, and estimates loadings in Beta like for second-order factors:
>
> lavInspect(fit5c, "est") # lambda is identity for x1-x5, theta is zero
>
> So although the model specification may not be identical, you can still check whether the specifications in lavaan and Mplus are equivalent (such that the two representations would lead to identical model-implied Sigma).  If their specifications are equivalent, I would still assume any difference between their point/SE estimates must be due to differences in the estimation algorithm.
>
> > > "If a model is truly not empirically identified, it is often still possible to find a local solution."
> >
> > But here you refer to the problem whether or not the model is empiricallly identified or unidentified. ... Such problems do not appear in the model (I believe). Besides, usually a program will give a warning if this is going on; for example, the program finds a solution, but also mentions that the SEs cannot be computed or should not be trusted. Or the SEs are huge, for instance.
>
> Right, like this clearly underidentified model, which even has negative df
>
> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 '
> fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, auto.var = TRUE)
> lavInspect(fit, "converged") ## no SEs, but still "converged"
>
> But I am not so certain that there isn't some mysterious empirical identification issue.  For instance, if you fit model5c again (that we both assume is underidentified because x5 freely predicts x1-x4 as well as f1), using the model-implied moments from fit5c, you will get the same estimates and SEs.  This is no surprise, given that fit5c perfectly reproduces the data ($\chi^2$ == 0).
>
> summary(fit5c)
> summary(update(fit5c, sample.cov = lavInspect(fit5c, "cov.ov"), sample.cov.rescale = FALSE))
>
> But if you identify the measurement model by fixing the factor's (residual) variance instead of the first loading, then you get the expected warning message you mentioned, that SEs could not be computed:
>
> summary(update(fit5c, model = 'f1~x5;  f1=~x1+x2+x3+x4 ; x1+x2+x3+x4~x5', sample.cov = lavInspect(fit5c, "cov.ov"), sample.cov.rescale = FALSE, std.lv = TRUE))
>
> Yet this is a statistically equivalent model, verified by the fact that its chi-squared is also 0, with 1 df.
>
> > I won't exclude the possibility that the model was empirically unidentified, but I ought the possibility small (especially since lavaan gave smaller SEs in the situation the chances were the greatest this problem might have occurred).
>
> Well, we both expected model5c to be underidentified (despite positive df), but it seems to be empirically identified for some reason.  I wondered whether lack of sampling error had anything to do with the optimizer's ability to find a solution, but even if sampling from cmatb, nlminb() finds a solution and computes SEs.
>
> temp <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(500, mu = rep(0, 5), Sigma = cmatb))
> summary(update(fit5c, data = temp, sample.cov = NULL))
>
>
> So I am as stumped as you are.  If you can fit model5c in Mplus and print TECH1 output, perhaps post that output here as an attachment to help verify whether the model specifications are at least equivalent.  I think Mplus will still print TECH1 even if the model does not converge.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much Terrence!
May you help me with the second question:

"Furthermore, I want to analyze the correlation between the latent constructs of both groups."

I get the correlation coefficients of both groups in the summary of my analysis. But where do I get the information about the significance level of the differences between both groups?

Greetings

Am Mittwoch, 8. März 2017 12:41:38 UTC+1 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:
> > Regarding the two subgroups they are partial strict invariant.
>
> Hopefully that means you have 2 invariant indicators, because there is no way to test whether 1 indicator is invariant (all models with 1 invariant item would be statistically equivalent).  Of course, strict invariance is not required for testing latent parameters anyway.  Only invariant loadings are required for testing latent (co)variances, but intercepts are also required for testing latent means.
>
> > Now I want to compare the latent means of both groups and analyze if they are statistical significant different.
> > Furthermore, I want to analyze the correlation between the latent constructs of both groups.
> > For this analyze I want to use the SEM. May anyone help me?
>
> Same way, by testing model constraints.  Those parameters should be freely estimated in your partial-strict-invariance model.  So if you fit a model where you add the constraint that latent means are equal (e.g., fixing the means to zero in both groups instead of only the first group), then you test that null hypothesis with a chi-squared difference test returned by anova() or lavTestLRT().  You can constrain a latent mean or covariance to equality across groups by assigning a parameter the same label within each group.
>
> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html  (see Constraining a single parameter to be equal across groups)
>
> Or if you only have 2 groups and the latent mean is only estimated in the second, then that parameter estimate is already "how different from zero" it is, so you can look at the Wald z for that parameter to test whether it equals zero (the first group's mean).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Elisabeth

messages.subject: Re: Measurement Invariance - comparison of means across groups
messages.subject_clean: Measurement Invariance - comparison of means across groups
messages.body_plain:
> where do I get the information about the significance level of the differences between both groups?

Same way, by testing model constraints.  To specifically test the correlation, you need to make sure the common factors have the same variance across groups.  There are 2 options:
Fit a model with latent variances constrained to equality.  (1a) If you identify the configural model by fixing factor variances to 1, you should have freed the variances in all but 1 group after constraining loadings to equality.  So constraining the factor variances to equality would mean fixing them all to 1 again.  (1b) If, on the other hand, you identify the configural model by fixing a factor loading to 1, your factor variances are all freely estimated, so you test equality of variances by giving parameters the same label in your syntax.  I would not recommend (1b) because you have to assume that the loadings fixed to 1 are invariance, which means you cannot test that assumption.
Specify a 2nd-order construct for each 1st-order construct, using the usual rules for single-indicator identification (fix variance of 1st-order factor to 0, fix variance of 2nd-order factor to 1, estimate "loading" in all groups except the first, which are fixed to 1 for identification).  Also fix the 1st-order factor covariance to zero, and they do not covary with 2nd-order factors.  The covariance(s) between 2nd-order factors will then be in correlation metric because the factor variances will all be 1.
Either way (1a, 1b, or 2), you compare the fit of the unconstrained model (free covariances between groups) to the fit of the model with the additional constraint that a covariance is equal across groups, by giving that parameter the same label in each group.  Then you test that null hypothesis with a chi-squared difference test returned by anova() or lavTestLRT().

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

And you can see which variables fall into certain categories using the ?lavNames function to print names of all vs. purely endogenous latent variables.

>From your path diagrams and syntax, I can't quite figure out why the first model's output includes estimates of diff10~~diff20, since those are endogenous but also predict stress1 and stress2. No, it did not.  You can see in the sessionInfo() output that you are still running version 0.4-14 (on CRAN).

The problem is that I pointed people to a *.tar.gz source file, which does not appear to be working anymore for R version 3.3.3 (since I built it using an earlier 3.3 version).  I did that to save people a little bit of time, but the safer way (which just worked for me using the latest R 3.3.3 and lavaan 0.6-1.1112) is to install directly from github using the devtools package:

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

That will take a little more time, but still less than a minute to install.  For those of you who just posted problems, please try this again in a fresh R session.  If it does not work, please also run sessionInfo() and post all of your console output.

>  perhaps there is a better way to run MI with flexibility in the various lavaan estimators.

runMI() should work with all the estimators described on the ?lavOptions help page.  From the error message I can see semTools 0.4-14 is still installed, because the development version does not have any trace of the old lavaanStar object.

It is necessary for the development version of lavaan to be installed before the development version of semTools can be installed, so make sure to install them in this order:

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

I haven't tried it on my Mac, but it shouldn't be a problem when installing from source / github (assuming you have R >= 3.3 installed).

> Thank you again for your help. I have restarted R and the problem persists. The problems is not there when  I use "fiml" instead of imputation.

All you posted was FIML output.  Did you get the same exact error message about not finding the "coef" method for "lavaan.mi"?  I have the same sessionInfo() output as you (except English instead of Spanish), and the example on the runMI() help page works fine for me.  Can you try the help page examples?  If it is an issue with your data, I may need a copy of some of it to reproduce your error.

Note that if you are using RStudio, you many notice a message like this when you launch it:

[Workspace loaded from ~/.../.RData]

This indicates that you are saving your workspace, which is automatically being loaded when you start RStudio again.  That means whatever packages were loaded will be loaded again.  This is an unfortunate default setting in RStudio.  If this is happening, here is how to stop it:
Click on Tools --> Global Options
Uncheck the box that says "Restore .RData into workspace at startup"
In the drop-down menu by "Save workspace to .RData on exit:", choose "Never"
click OK
Delete the hidden ".RData" file from your working directory
Shut down RStudio, restart it, and you should not see any message about loading a workspace

messages.body_plain:
OK, this script "works" for me, in the sense that I don't get the errors you saw when I run it using the latest versions available.  In a fresh R session, install all 3 packages:

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/simsem/simsem")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Now, I still got an error, but not from simsem.  Your population model is not possible, in the sense that the model-implied covariance matrix is not positive definite.  A good trick to check whether you have specified a plausible set of parameters is to check the model-implied population covariance matrix:

(impliedSigma <- fitted(lavaan(mod1.pop2)))

Using your script above, you will notice this error:

> Error in lav_start_check_cov(lavpartable = lavpartable, start = START) :
>   lavaan ERROR: please provide better fixed values for (co)variances;
>                 variables involved are: bem eg
> In addition: Warning message:
> In lav_start_check_cov(lavpartable = lavpartable, start = START) :
>   lavaan WARNING: starting values imply a correlation larger than 1;
>                   variables involved are: bem eg

The first problem it notices are with bem and eg, but I don't think those are the only problematic parameters.  After changing these 2 parameters:

> bem ~~ .3*eg
> bem ~~ .1*sr

I still got a warning that Sigma is not positive definite, so it is still not possible to draw samples from that population. You can check yourself that the determinant is negative:

det(fitted(lavaan(mod1.pop2))$cov)

You can keep adjusting the population values until you get a positive determinant.  Since you are specifying the population using lavaan syntax, you can also check whether the population is acceptable by using lavaan's simulateData() function to see whether you can draw one sample from it.

simulateData(mod1.pop2, sample.nobs = 10)

If you can, then you should be able to provide that same script to simsem.

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: (bootstrapLavaan) Error in Yc[case.idx, var.idx, drop = FALSE] : subscript out of bounds
messages.subject_clean: (bootstrapLavaan) Error in Yc[case.idx, var.idx, drop = FALSE] : subscript out of bounds
messages.body_plain:
> > Error in Yc[case.idx, var.idx, drop = FALSE] : subscript out of bounds

This has to do with some newer source code (see file: lav_mvnorm_missing.R).

Pragmatically speaking, why are you requesting a robust estimator if you are bootstrapping?  In fact, the only fit measure you are requesting is the naïve chi-squared, so you don't need to request MLR or missing = pairwise.  You can just use FIML to get a bootstrap distribution of that statistic (not that it varies at all in this case, since your model has df = 0).

Of course, the results will not really represent the distribution of that statistic under the null hypothesis, even if the data were normal, because you are bootstrapping from data which were (almost certainly) generated from a different population than the one implied by your model's estimates (i.e., the null is false).  The solution to this is to transform the data, commonly referred to as the Bollen-Stine (1992) transformation, which is only available using complete data.  You can request a Bollen-Stine bootstrap in the semTools package, and your top example works in the latest development version (make sure the devtools package is installed):

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

dat <- read.table("data_error_bootstrap.dat", header = TRUE)
library(semTools)

model <- 'x =~ x1 + x2 + x3'

fit <- cfa(model=model, data=dat, missing="FIML", estimator = "MLR")
out <- bsBootMiss(fit, nBoot = 10)
summary(out)

Another curiosity of your example is that there is in fact only complete data and completely missing data, so missing = "fiml" returns the same output as missing = "listwise" would.

lavInspect(fit, "patterns")

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: bootstrapLRT: problem in understanding
messages.subject_clean: bootstrapLRT: problem in understanding
messages.body_plain:
> since the null hypothesis (r = 1.00) corresponds to the boundary of the parameter space, the asymptotic distribution of the Chi^2 distribution is not a standard Chi^2 distribution but a mixture of such distributions ...).

I think your reviewer is mistaken.  The optimizer has no idea that parameters have any boundaries whatsoever; that is a constraint we add to our interpretation of the estimated parameters.  Fixing the correlation to 1 does not result in a mixture of chi-squareds any more than fixing the residual variance of a single-indicator does.  I think the situation the reviewer has in mind is if the estimation algorithm returns a Heywood case, and you try to "fix" that problem with an inequality constraint to force that estimated (not fixed) parameter to be within certain boundaries -- that will result in a mixture of chi-squareds

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

You can post this question on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> too, if you want some additional verification before telling a reviewer they might be mistaken :-)

> What are the LRT values and how should I use these values? As they are sometimes > 1 I guess they are not p-values

They are LRT values (the chi-squared statistic evaluated after fitting the model to each bootstrap sample).  See the ?bootstrapLRT help page for the description of the (unnecessary) return.LRT argument.  Your p value is just above the attributes, and just below the (also unnecessary) verbosity.  If you leave out those arguments, you can see the p value more clearly because it will be the only thing printed.  Note that you should use the Bollen-Stine transformation instead of a simple parametric bootstrap, to ensure your data are resampled under a true null hypothesis.  (Assuming you still decide to use bootstrapping -- there is nothing wrong with including both results.)

bootstrapLRT(h0 = fit.b, h1 = fit.a, R = 2000, type = "bollen.stine",
             parallel = "snow", ncpus = parallel::detectCores() - 1L)

Note I also used the parallel options to decrease computation time, but that is entirely optional.  If you have a Mac or Linux operating system, parallel = "multicore" should be even more efficient.

The estimated probability of observing your chi-squared difference statistic if the null were true (i.e., the p value) is the proportion of the bootstrap distribution that exceeds the observed statistic.  This is the same as using the theoretical chi-squared distribution, but you use an empirical distribution based on the data instead of relying on asymptotic normal theory.  The vector of LRT values you asked about are the empirical distribution used to calculate the p value.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> whether the syntax is correct or not?

Looks correct, does it work?  Two notes:
There is no need to mean-center your predictors, but if you insist on doing so, you should be consistent and use the mean-centered predictors x and z in addition to the product of the mean-centered variables. Otherwise your interpretation is messed up by the not being able to hold x (or z) constant at a particular level (e.g., 0 would be "at the mean" for the product term, but actually zero for the simple effect).
As far as I know, the standardized solution will not result in correct standardized coefficients because lavaan must assume "xz" is a variable all its own, not a product of 2 other variables.  To get correct standardized coefficients, manually save standardized versions of your variables in the data set, calculate the product term from those, then fit the model to the standardized data (pay attention only to the coefficients, which will be standardized; pay no attention to the SEs or significance tests).
pathdata$x.st <- scale(pathdata$x)
pathdata$m.st <- scale(pathdata$m)
pathdata$y.st <- scale(pathdata$y)
pathdata$z.st <- scale(pathdata$z)
pathdata$xz.st <- pathdata$x.st * pathdata$z.st

stmodel <- ' m.st <http://m.st> ~ x.st <http://x.st> + z.st <http://z.st> + xz.st <http://xz.st>
             y.st <http://y.st> ~ x.st <http://x.st> + z.st <http://z.st> + m.st <http://m.st> + xz.st <http://xz.st> '
stpathfit <- sem(stmodel, pathdata)
coef(stpathfit) # standardized coefficients

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> > Do you recall a way to display R2-squared values for this? (to evaluate how much variance the full model explained).

>
> > What do you mean by "approximately continuous"? Is there a statistical way to check for that?
>
> Not in a hypothesis-testing way, but there are practical guidelines you might be able to find with a little Googling.  I think a Poisson distribution is approximately normalish when the mean is as little as 10 or 15.  Binomial (not binary) variables are approximately normal when they are based on at least 30 trials.  But continuity should be good enough, even if not normal, because there are robust estimators that adjust for excess kurtosis.  Ordinal data can be treated as continuous when there are at least 5 categories, or at least 7 if the distributions are quite skewed.  Here is some helpful reading, although it is about ordinal data, not counts per se.
>
> http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been experiencing an issue running multiple group analysis with recent version of lavaan. Basically, I receive an error message if I include a 'group.label' argument in my code.

A reproducible example:

Let say I aim to replicate the Holzinger and Swineford analysis for multiple groups -- in this case, the two different schools in the data.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model

HS.model <- '
             visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
             textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
             speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
            '

## If I just include 'group', everything works fine.

fit1 <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
               group="school",
               auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
               auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit1, fit.measures=TRUE)

## However, if I name the groups using 'group.label', I receive an error message like:

fit2 <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              group="school", group.label=c("Pasteur","Grant-White"),
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)

Error in lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan ERROR: no group levels left; check the group.label argument
In addition: Warning message:
In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some group.labels do not appear in the grouping variable: pasteur grant-white
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As trivial as this might go --in this example I could just get rid of 'group.label' and I would obtain the same results-- things get a bit more complicate if, for instance, I set Grant-White as the reference group using ' group.label=c("Grant-White", "Pasteur")' in measurement invariance study.

Is there any change in how to use group.label in the most recent lavaan version? I used to use group.label to re-order groups in the analysis (to set a different group as the reference rather than the group that occurs first in the dataset). I could run codes like this in the recent past but tried to re-run my analyses now (after updating packages) and got this message so I guess there are changes in how lavaan handles group.label arguments.

Hi all,

after searching this group and the internet I still haven't found an answer to my question and hopefully, you might be able to help me out.
I've set up the following multigroup SEM, which gives good fit indices.

sem_model <- "f1 =~ indf11_z + indf12_z + indf13_z

f2 =~ indf21_z + indf22_z + indf23_z + indf24_z

f3 =~ indf31_z + indf32_z + indf33_z

f4 =~ indf41_z + indf42_z + indf43_z

f5 =~ indf51_z + indf52_z + indf53_z

f6 =~ indf61_z + indf62_z + indf63_z

f7 =~ indf71_z + indf72_z + indf73_z

f8 =~ indf81_z + indf82_z + indf83_z + indf84_z

f3 ~ f1 + f2 + f8

f4 ~ f1 + f2 + f8

f5 ~ f1 + f2 + f8

f6 ~ F1 + f2 + f8

f3 ~~ f4 + f5 + f6

f4 ~~ f5 + f6

f5 ~~ f6

f1 ~~ f8 + f2

f2 ~~ f8

f7 ~ f2 + f1 + f8 + f3 + f4 + f5 + f6"

fit_sem_model <- sem(sem_model, data = cfa_data, group = "agegr", missing = "fiml", estimator = "MLR")

Now I want to compare path coefficients between the two groups which I do by restraining the variable of interest (see below, e.g. difference in f1 on f3):

f1_on_f3_model <- "f1 =~ indf11_z + indf12_z + indf13_z

f2 =~ indf21_z + indf22_z + indf23_z + indf24_z

f3 =~ indf31_z + indf32_z + indf33_z

f4 =~ indf41_z + indf42_z + indf43_z

f5 =~ indf51_z + indf52_z + indf53_z

f6 =~ indf61_z + indf62_z + indf63_z

f7 =~ indf71_z + indf72_z + indf73_z

f8 =~ indf81_z + indf82_z + indf83_z + indf84_z

f3 ~ c(compare, compare)*f1 + f2 + f8

f4 ~ f1 + f2 + f8

f5 ~ f1 + f2 + f8

f6 ~ F1 + f2 + f8

f3 ~~ f4 + f5 + f6

f4 ~~ f5 + f6

f5 ~~ f6

f1 ~~ f8 + f2

f2 ~~ f8

f7 ~ f2 + f1 + f8 + f3 + f4 + f5 + f6"

fit_model_f1_on_f3 <- sem(f1_on_f3_model, data = cfa_data, group = "agegr", missing = "fiml", estimator = "MLR")

lavTestLRT(fit_sem_model, fit_model_f1_on_f3) # test for significance (satorra.bentler.2001)

lavTestLRT(fit_sem_model, fit_model_f1_on_f3, method = "satorra.bentler.2010") # test for significance in case scaling factor is negative

When I have to use satorra.bentler.2010 I sometimes get a p-value of 1, which makes me wonder if the correction has worked or this may be some sort of mistake. My second question is then, how to properly use the sb-correction (for reporting it in an article). Do I go with the 2001-version unless the scaling factor is negative in which case I use sb2010 or do i have to use one version for all comparisons due to consistency reasons (in my case this would then be sb2010)? Any advice is dearly appreciated!

Thanks,

Eva

messages.subject: Re: Getting modification indices for all but the right variables
messages.subject_clean: Getting modification indices for all but the right variables
messages.body_plain:
> I'm exploring the validity of a 58 ordinal item questionnaire.

Wow!  I hope you have a magnificently large sample.

> When I request the modindices, I get values for all but the items that were made to load onto the factors. That is, for Boldness I get mod indices for the items that load on Meanness and Disinhibition. On the other hand, with the CFA example on the lavaan website, which used a similar model,the mod indices were displayed as they should: only for the items that load onto their own factors. What is the difference and how can I fix it?

That doesn't make sense.  What you are describing with your own data are what you should see.  Modification indices are (and should be) returned only for parameters that are fixed to zero (i.e., cross-loadings that you do not estimate) because you can't free a parameter that is already freely estimated. And that is what is returned by the lavaan example:

example(modindices, package = "lavaan")

If you are looking for modification indices for equality-constrained estimated parameters, they are not returned by modindices(), but can be investigated using the lavTestScore() function.

HS.model <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
    speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
           group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts"))
lavTestScore(fit)
## see which constraints are associated with each label
parTable(fit)

messages.subject_clean: MLR scaling correction factor = NA
messages.body_plain:
> Is there anyway to prevent my model (below) from going back to using OLS estimation and instead use ML estimation?
>
> Mod1.3 <- 'SA10 ~ IQ.all + SES.all + SA7 + SCDiff7 + Friend.all + Friend.all:SCDiff7'

You can use Wald chi-squared tests by fitting the full model with each parameter (that you intend to test) labeled.  You then test 1 or more effects equaling zero by specifying those constraints in the lavTestWald() function.  Because the interaction term apparently MUST remain in your model for it to converge, you can test lower-order effects by fixing both it/they and the interaction effect to zero.  For example:

mod.full <- ' x9 ~ b1*x1 + b2*x2 + b3*x3 + b23*x2:x3 '
fit.full <- sem(mod.full, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "MLR")
summary(fit.full)

lavTestWald(fit.full, constraints = 'b1 == 0') # test effect of x1
lavTestWald(fit.full, constraints = 'b23 == 0') # test interaction effect

# simultaneously test interaction effect and one lower-order effect
lavTestWald(fit.full, constraints = 'b23 == 0 ; b2 == 0')
# simultaneously test interaction effect and the other lower-order effect
lavTestWald(fit.full, constraints = 'b23 == 0 ; b3 == 0')
# simultaneously test interaction effect and both lower-order effects
lavTestWald(fit.full, constraints = 'b23 == 0 ; b2 == 0 ; b3 == 0')

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Direction of trait scale
messages.subject_clean: Direction of trait scale
messages.body_plain:
> When I compute binary indicator thresholds using glm they have the opposite sign to thresholds computed by lavaan.

glm() does not estimate a threshold, it estimates the intercept.  Because your glm() model has not predictors, it's intercept is the grand "mean", or the z score corresponding to an overall probability that x1 == 1.

> Is the scale direction arbitrary or is there some reason why these signs are opposite?

For binary data, threshold == -1 * intercept (similar sign-switching equality for more ordered categories).  If you override the defaults, you can estimate intercepts instead of thresholds for your latent item responses.

tau0.nuFree <- c(' trait =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 ',
                 paste0("x", 1:9, " | 0*t1"),
                 paste0("x", 1:9, " ~ NA*1"))
out <- cfa(tau0.nuFree, data=dat, ordered=names(dat), std.lv <http://std.lv/>=TRUE)
summary(out)

Notice the intercepts match your glm() output.  So yes, it is in a sense arbitrary whether you fix thresholds and estimate intercepts or vice versa, because the parameterizations lead to equivalent implications (model-implied probabilities and tetrachoric correlations).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Interconstruct Correlation Greater than 1
messages.subject_clean: Interconstruct Correlation Greater than 1
messages.body_plain:
> My issue is that the factor correlations (stability and plasticity) are greater than 1 when estimated freely. In other words, I have a non-positive definite matrix. I'm looking for advice for overcoming this issue.

Have you considered the possibility that your hypothesis is wrong?  The fact that the estimated correlation exceeds 1 indicates that at least one pair of first-order factors (indicators from different second-order factors) are more correlated than the simple second-order structure allows for.  You could look at the latent covariance matrix from a model with only first-order factors for clues.

Model misfit is only one possible cause of a Heywood case. Another is sampling error.  At smaller sample sizes, you can expect Heywood cases if the true parameter is near a boundary.  You have a pretty big sample size, though.  But you can check whether the null hypothesis is plausible that the true parameter is an acceptable value.  Check your CI, and you will notice it includes (barely) includes some plausible correlations below 1, indicating the data are also consistent with a true correlation of, e.g., 0.995. So although you cannot disregard sampling error as the cause of the Heywood case (nor model misfit as the cause), the CI still indicates that if your model is correct, your data are only consistent with a true correlation very near the boundary, in which case you could try a 1-factor solution as well.  But I would recommend inspecting the first-order factor correlations for clues as to how your hypothesized 2-factor structure might not be appropriate.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
